title: Reflection and Attributes
summary: Let a program inspect its own types at run time, and tag code with metadata that other code can read.

steps.title: Types are objects too
body: While a program runs, .NET keeps a description of every type in it. **Reflection** lets you read those descriptions. The entry point is the `Type` class, and there are two ways to get one:
Type a = typeof(string);        // from a type name, known at compile time
Type b = value.GetType();       // from an object, discovered at run time
`GetType()` reports what the object *really* is, no matter what type the variable has. That is why `b.Name` is `Int32` and not `Object`.
Notice the name: reflection shows the .NET names. `int` is `Int32`, `string` is `String`, `bool` is `Boolean`, `double` is `Double`.

steps.explain: Every variable here is an `object`, but `GetType()` looks at the actual value. The names are the .NET names behind the C# keywords.

steps.title: Reading members and invoking them
body: A `Type` can list its members. Most of these classes live in `System.Reflection`.
var book = new Book { Title = "Dune", Pages = 412 };
A `PropertyInfo` describes a property *in general*. To read it you say which object to read it from: `prop.GetValue(book)`. The result is an `object`.
Methods work the same way. Find one by name, then invoke it on an object with an array of arguments:
object? result = method.Invoke("reflection", new object[] { "flec" });    // True
This code never mentions `Title` or `Pages`. It works for any object you hand it. That is the point of reflection.

steps.title: Custom attributes
body: An **attribute** is a label you attach to code in square brackets. You have seen built-in ones such as `[Obsolete]`. You can make your own: write a class that derives from `Attribute`.
- By convention the class name ends in `Attribute`, and you leave that suffix off when you apply it.
- `[AttributeUsage(...)]` says where the label may be placed.
An attribute **does nothing on its own**. It is a note stuck to the property. Something has to come along and read it, with reflection:
`GetCustomAttribute<T>()` returns `null` when the member does not carry that attribute.

steps.prompt: A property is marked `[MaxLength(20)]`, and no code anywhere reads that attribute. What happens when you assign it a 50-character string?
options: Nothing special. The string is stored; an attribute is only metadata
The string is cut down to 20 characters
steps.explain: Attributes are passive. They only have an effect when some code, yours or a framework's, looks for them and acts on what it finds.

steps.title: What reflection costs
body: Serializers, test frameworks, dependency injection containers and validation libraries are all built on reflection and attributes. It is powerful, and it has a price.
- **It is slow.** Reading a property through `GetValue` is many times slower than `book.Title`. Looking members up by name is slower still.
- **The compiler cannot help you.** `type.GetProperty("Titel")` compiles happily and returns `null` at run time.
- **Renames break it silently.** Rename `Title` and the string `"Title"` stays behind.
- Use reflection at the edges of a program (loading, saving, validating input), not in a tight loop.
- Look things up once and keep the `PropertyInfo` if you need it again.
- Prefer `nameof(Book.Title)` to the string `"Title"`. It is checked by the compiler.

steps.prompt: `Book` has a `string Title` and an `int Pages`. If each line contains a mistake, when do you find out?
buckets: It fails only when it runs
steps.explain: Anything written as real C# is checked by the compiler. Anything hidden in a string, or behind `object`, is only checked when that line actually runs.

steps.title: A mini validator
prompt: Two attributes are ready in the starter: `[NotEmpty]` and `[Between(min, max)]`. They do nothing yet. Make them mean something.
Complete `Validator.Validate(object obj)`. It looks at every public property of `obj` and returns a list of error messages:
- a property marked `[NotEmpty]` whose value is `null`, empty or only spaces adds `"{Name} is required"`
- a property marked `[Between(min, max)]` whose `int` value is outside `min..max` (the limits themselves are allowed) adds `"{Name} must be between {min} and {max}"`
A valid object gives an empty list. For example the harness has:
and `Validate(new Signup { Name = "", Age = 12 })` returns `Name is required` and `Age must be between 18 and 120`.
starter: public BetweenAttribute(int min, int max) { Min = min; Max = max; }

solution: public BetweenAttribute(int min, int max) { Min = min; Max = max; }
if (between != null && value is int number && (number < between.Min || number > between.Max))
template: using System.Reflection;
string __Errors(object o) => string.Join(" | ", Validator.Validate(o).OrderBy(e => e, StringComparer.Ordinal));
void __Case(string name, string expected, object o) => Dojo.Try(name, () => Dojo.Eq(name, expected, __Errors(o)));
__Case("A valid signup has no errors", "", new Signup { Name = "Ana", Age = 30 });
__Case("An empty Name is reported", "Name is required", new Signup { Name = "", Age = 30 });
__Case("A null Name is reported", "Name is required", new Signup { Name = null, Age = 30 });
__Case("An Age of 12 is reported", "Age must be between 18 and 120", new Signup { Name = "Ben", Age = 12 });
__Case("The limits 18 and 120 are allowed", "", new Signup { Name = "Cy", Age = 18 });
__Case("Two problems give two errors", "Age must be between 18 and 120 | Name is required", new Signup { Name = "  ", Age = 200 });
__Case("It works for a different class: Product", "Stock must be between 0 and 999", new Product { Sku = "T-1", Stock = -1, Note = "" });
class Signup
[NotEmpty] public string? Name { get; set; }
[Between(18, 120)] public int Age { get; set; }
class Product
[NotEmpty] public string? Sku { get; set; }
[Between(0, 999)] public int Stock { get; set; }
public string? Note { get; set; }

hints: Loop with `foreach (PropertyInfo prop in obj.GetType().GetProperties())` and read `object? value = prop.GetValue(obj);`.
`prop.GetCustomAttribute<NotEmptyAttribute>() != null` tells you the property is marked. `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value as string)` covers null, empty and spaces.
For the range: `var between = prop.GetCustomAttribute<BetweenAttribute>();` then `if (between != null && value is int n && (n < between.Min || n > between.Max))`.
